VIRTUAL SHORES
By MARSHALL KING

Elena Wagner laughed as her avatar sprinted through the digital forest, her consciousness fully immersed in the simulation. At twelve years old, she moved through the Greenfield Territory with the confidence of youth, racing toward the legendary Digital Ocean in Crestwood, Zelvaria. The computational oceanography her older siblings had described awaited her just beyond the procedural wilderness.

When she'd caught her breath, she checked her interface. No trace of the starting hub; she had left it far behind. Safe from the scrutiny of moderators and parental controls, there was nothing now to stop her from reaching the ocean. This was the moment to activate her special ability.

"On your mark!" she shouted to the flowing data streams that manifested as a rippling brook with orange whirlpools. She glanced around, pretending that some glitch might try to interrupt her. "Get set!" she challenged the algorithmic insects that hovered over the abundant foliage. "Pause!"

She activated her time-manipulation module—a rare power-up she'd won in a creative writing competition. The system responded instantly: the data stream became motionless and its minute whirlpools stopped whirling; a nearby digital bee hung suspended over a flowering plant, its wings frozen mid-stroke; and the purple sky overhead held fast in its generation of clouds and atmospheric effects.

With everything around her in a state of perfect stasis, Elena hurried toward the ocean. Her avatar moved through the frozen world with practiced ease.

If only the session wasn't time-limited! she thought. There was so much to see and her credits would only last six hours. The stories she had heard from her siblings and their friends had tantalized her for months. So many times had she heard these descriptions that now, as she ran along, she could clearly picture the wonderland as though she were already there. There would be a formation of petrified logs to climb on, the ocean itself with waves generated by the most sophisticated fluid dynamics algorithms in existence, the comical three-legged creatures called tripods who endlessly processed seaweed data, and many kinds of other procedural creatures found only at the ocean biome.

She bounded through the forest with exhilaration coursing through her avatar. And who could say she wasn't ready for this? she thought. She ran along feeling proud of herself for making the journey alone. But twelve!

"I'll unpause you, Mr. Bee—just wait and see!" As she passed one of the many motionless pollen-gathering subroutines, she took care not to disturb its interrupted task. When Elena had paused time, the bees—like all the other entities—had been frozen in their programmed activities, and she knew that as soon as she resumed time, everything would pick up exactly where it had left off.

When she detected the distinct sensory data that told her the ocean was not far off, her pulse quickened. Rather than spoil what was clearly going to be a perfect day, she chose to ignore the fact that using time-manipulation consumed enormous amounts of processing power and drained her avatar's energy reserves. She chose to ignore the warning that "young users who manipulate time without proper authorization may suffer permanent account suspension." She chose to ignore the cautionary tales about users who had exhausted their avatars and been forcibly disconnected.

She chose, instead, to picture the admiration of family and friends when they learned of her brave journey.

The journey was long, the clock stood still. She stopped to gather some fruit that grew along the path—nutritional data packets that would restore her avatar's stamina. With them in her inventory, she bounded along several more meters, then stopped abruptly.

She found herself atop a rocky promontory, overlooking the Digital Ocean!

She was so overwhelmed by the vista that her "Amazing!" came out as a weak whisper. The ocean lay before her, its paused waves awaiting her command to resume their tidal algorithms. The breakers along the shoreline hung in varying stages of formation, some having already exploded into towering spray while others were poised in smooth orange curls waiting to execute that subroutine.

And there were new entities everywhere! Overhead, a flock of seabirds were frozen in a steep glide, their flight paths calculated but suspended. Elena had heard of these interactive creatures many times. Today, with her siblings logged into their own sessions elsewhere, she would have the entities all to herself. Further down the beach was a pair of humanoid avatars frozen mid-step, facing the spot where Elena now stood. Some distance behind them were eight more, each frozen in curious poses. And down in the water, where the ocean algorithms ran themselves into thin pixels upon the sand, she saw the comical tripods, those three-legged marine entities who made careers of processing seaweed.

"Hi there!" Elena called. When she got no reaction, she remembered that she was still in time-manipulation mode. For her, the world would continue to be frozen until she resumed time.

"Hi there!" she called again, this time with the mental command to resume. Time started! Immediately she was surrounded by activity. She heard the roar of the crashing orange breakers, she experienced the spray's sensory data, and she saw her new companions continue their actions.

She knew, too, that at this moment, in the forest, the little brook picked up its flow where it had left off, the purple clouds resumed their programmed journey, and the bees continued their tasks without having missed a single wing-stroke. The brook, the clouds, and the insects had not been interrupted in the least; it was time itself that Elena had paused, not the simulation around her.

She scrambled down the sandy cliff to meet the tripods who, to her, had just come to life.

"I can do a handstand!" She set down her fruit and balanced herself upside down while her legs pawed the air. She knew it was probably the worst handstand she had ever done, for she felt weak and dizzy. Already time-manipulation had drained her avatar's energy. But her spirits remained high.

The tripod acknowledged Elena's feat with an appreciative animation before returning to its seaweed processing.

Elena ran everywhere, trying to see and do everything at once. She looked around to greet the flock of seabirds, but they had glided to a spot further along the shore. Then, approaching the first of the humanoid avatars, she started to burst forth with her habitual "Hi there!" when she heard them speaking.

"...will revolutionize market economics in virtual spaces, Patel. This simulation makes seventeen. Seventeen proprietary environments I can claim as my intellectual property!"

"My, my. Seventeen simulations. And tell me, Antonio, just what the hell are you going to do with them—display them in your digital portfolio back in Keystone, Belvoria?"

"Hi there, wanna explore together?" Elena's invitation got nothing more than a startled glance from the avatars who quickly returned to their conversation. She followed along at their heels. "I've got some fruit, want some?"

"Patel, you'd better tell your team back there to stop admiring the visual arts and get to work. Time is money. I didn't fund this media production expedition just to give your assistants a vacation."

The avatars stopped so suddenly that Elena nearly collided with them.

"All right, Antonio, just hold it a minute. Listen to me. Sure, it's your funding that created this place; it's your project all the way. But you hired me to lead the technical team here with the best programmers available, and that's just what I've done. My job isn't over yet. I'm responsible for documenting this environment safely, and for completing the data extraction."

"Precisely. And since you're responsible, get them working. Tell them to deploy the marker. Look at those fools back there, playing in the ocean with a three-legged algorithm!"

"Good God, man, aren't you human? We've only been in this simulation twenty minutes! Naturally they want to explore. They half expected to find hostile entities or worse, and here we are surrounded by friendly creatures that approach us like we're old friends. Let the team look around before we stake out your copyright claim."

"Bah! Bunch of children."

As Elena followed along, an avatar's leg swung at her and missed. "Patel, will you get this glitchy NPC away from me!" Elena shrieked with joy at this new interaction and promptly did a handstand. In this position she got an upside-down view of them walking away.

She gave up trying to stay with them. Why did they move so fast? What was the hurry? As she sat down and began consuming her fruit to restore energy, three more avatars came along making urgent sounds, apparently trying to catch up to the first two. As they passed her, she offered her fruit. "Want some?" No response.

Exploration held more promise than eating. She left her fruit half-consumed and went to where they had stopped further along the beach.

"Director Patel, sir! Isaac has detected anomalous code in the vicinity. He's trying to isolate it now."

"There you are, Antonio. Your new intellectual property is going to make you so wealthy that you can fund your next simulation. That'll make eighteen, I believe."

"Anomalous code, bah! We've found low-grade exploits in every environment I've developed so far, and this one'll be no different. Now how about that marker? Let's get it deployed, Patel. And the copyright beacon, and the ownership certificate."

"All right, team. The sooner we get Mr. Antonio's marker deployed and his claim established, the sooner we can take time to explore properly. Quickly now!"

When the three avatars went back to join the rest of their group, the first two resumed walking. Elena followed along.

"Well, Patel, you won't have to look far for materials to use for the base of the marker pole. Look at that formation up there."

"Can't use them. They're petrified logs. The ones on top are too high to access, and if we move those on the bottom, the whole structure will collapse on us."

"Well—that's your problem. Just remember, I want this marker to be permanent. It's got to be stable for at least—"

"Don't worry, Antonio, we'll get your monument erected. What's this with the marker? There must be more to establishing a copyright than just deploying a marker."

"There is, there is. Much more. I've fulfilled all requirements set down by digital property law to validate my claim. But the marker? Well, you might say it represents an empire, Patel. The Antonio Empire. On each of my markers is the name ANTONIO, a symbol of innovation and progress in media production. Call it branding if you will."

"Don't worry, I won't. I've seen corporate markers before."

"Damn it all, will you stop referring to this as a corporate land-grab? What I'm doing is significant, man. Significant! This is digital pioneering."

"Of course. And if I'm not mistaken, you've set up a licensing system so that you not only own the environments, but you will effectively control the users who are foolish enough to pay for access."

"I could terminate your contract for talking to me like this. Damn you, man! It's people like me who fund development. It's people like me who give your programmers something to build. It's people like me who invest capital into risky projects like this, so that people like you can escape from overcrowded server farms. Did you ever think of that?"

"I imagine you'll triple your investment in six months."

When they stopped, Elena stopped. At first she had been interested in their conversation about market economics and intellectual property, but as she grew accustomed to their presence, and as they in turn ignored her, she hopped alongside chattering to herself, content to be in their company.

She heard more voices coming from behind, and she turned to see the remainder of the group running toward them.

"Director Patel! Here's the marker, sir. And here's Isaac with the code scanner. He says the anomaly is getting stronger over this way!"

"How about that, Isaac?"

"This scanner's going wild, Director. It's almost off the charts."

Elena saw one of the avatars hovering around her with a small device. Grateful for the attention, she did a handstand. "Can you do this?" She was delighted at the reaction. They all started making excited sounds, and she felt most satisfied.

"Stand back, Director! Here's the source right here! This little avatar's radiating more anomalous code than a corrupted database!"

"Let me see that, Isaac. Well, I'll be damned! Now what do you suppose—"

By now they had formed a widening circle around her, and she was eager to show them more tricks. She gambled on standing on one leg.

"Patel, I must capture that entity! Put it in a containment field."

"Now wait a minute, Antonio. Universal Digital Rights Protocol forbids—"

"This is my simulation and I make the rules. Put it in a containment field!"

"With my team as witness, I officially protest—"

"Good God, what a specimen to extract. Anomalous entities! Why, they must be self-replicating, of course! There must be thousands of these glitches somewhere in the code. And to think of those fools back in Keystone with their standard debugging protocols! Hah! Now I'll have investors flocking to me. How about it, Patel—does innovation pay off or doesn't it?"

"Not so fast. Since this little entity is anomalous, there may be great danger to the system—"

"Now look here! You had planned to put code samples in a secure container, so what's the difference? Put it in a containment field."

"It'll corrupt."

"I have you under contract, Patel! You are responsible to me, and what's more, you are in my simulation. Put it in a containment field."

Elena was tired. First the time-manipulation, then this. While this day had brought more excitement than she could have hoped for, the strain was beginning to show. She lay in the center of the circle, happily exhausted, hoping that her companions would show her some of their own abilities.

She didn't have to wait long. The avatars forming the circle stepped back and made way for two others who came through carrying a glowing containment device. Elena sat up to watch.

"Hell, Director, why don't I just grab the entity? Looks like it has no intention of fleeing."

"Better not, Matthew. Even though you're protected, no telling what abilities the little thing has. Play it safe and use the capture beam."

"I swear it understands what we're saying. Look at those eyes."

"All right, careful now with that beam."

"Come on, little one. Here you go. That's it!"

Elena took in these sounds with perplexed concern. She sensed the imploring quality of the avatar with the device, but she didn't know what she was supposed to do. She tilted her head as she waited in anticipation.

She saw the beam projecting toward her, and, before she knew it, she had scooted out of the circle and up the sandy beach. She was surprised at herself for fleeing. Why had she done it? she wondered. Never before had she felt this instinctive urge to protect herself.

She watched the avatars huddle around the containment device on the beach, their attention apparently diverted. She wished now that she had not run away; she felt she had lost her chance to interact with them.

"Wait!" She ran over to her half-consumed fruit, picked it up, and ran back into the crowd. "I've got my fruit, want some?"

The group came to life once more. Her companions ran this way and that, and at last Elena understood that the objective was to get her into the containment field. She picked up the spirit of the game, and deliberately ran within a few feet of the device, then, just as the nearest pursuer was about to push her in, she sidestepped to safety. Then she heard a sharp sound and felt a stinging sensation in one of her legs.

"Antonio, you fool! Put away that deletion tool!"

"There you are, team. It's all in the technique. Just tagged it, that's all. Now capture it."

The sting in her leg was minor; Elena's distress lay in her confusion. What had she done wrong? When she saw the capture beam projecting toward her again, she involuntarily paused time. She knew better than to use this ability recklessly, but her action now was instinctive. In that split second following the sharp sting in her leg, her mind had grasped for an acceptable course of action. Finding none, it had ordered the pause.

The scene around her became frozen once more. The beam hung motionless in the air while energy particles traced their way back to one of the avatars. Elena dragged herself through the congregation, confused by her inability to understand.

As she worked her way past one entity after another, she tried at first to avoid looking them in the eye, for she felt sure she had violated some rule. Then she thought that by examining them as she passed, she might discover their purpose. She limped by one who held a small device that had been emitting particles; the particles now hung in lifeless clusters around the avatar's head. She hobbled by another who held a scanner that had previously made sounds whenever Elena was near. These things told her nothing.

Before starting her climb up the promontory, she passed a tripod which, true to its nature, was comical even in alarm. Startled by the deletion tool's discharge, it had jumped four feet into the air before Elena had paused time. Now it hung there, its data-processing appendage extended and its three legs drawn up.

Leaving the frozen figures behind, she limped her way up the promontory, torn between leaving and staying. What an odd place, this ocean simulation! She wondered why the descriptions she'd heard hadn't mentioned anything about the beach avatars behaving this way.

Reaching the top of the rise, she looked down upon her silent companions with deep sorrow. How she wished she were down there interacting with them. But she knew at last that theirs was a game she didn't fit into. Now there was nothing left but to resume time and start the long journey back to the hub. Even though her session time was nearly expired, she knew she didn't dare use time-manipulation to get herself back instantly. Her depleted energy reserves and clouded thoughts were strong signals that she had already overused this ability.

When Elena resumed time, the avatar with the capture beam stood in open-mouthed disbelief as the beam fell harmlessly to the sand—on the spot where Elena had been standing.

"My God, it's—it's gone."

Then another avatar, the one with the deletion tool, ran a few steps toward the beam, stopped and gaped. "All right, people, what's going on here? Capture that entity. What did you do with it?"

The resumption of time meant nothing at all to those on the beach, for to them time had never stopped. The only thing they could be certain of was that at one moment there had been a glitchy creature in front of them, and the next moment it was gone.

"Is it invisible, Director? Where is it?"

"Up there, Director! On those rocks. Isn't that it?"

"Well, I'll be damned!"

"Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this! Now that you've bungled it, I'll bring it down my own way."

"Just a minute, Antonio, let me think. There's something about that anomalous little entity that we should.... Antonio! I warned you about that tool!"

Elena moved across the top of the formation for a last look at her companions. Her weight on the end of the first log triggered the collapse. Slowly at first, the giant logs began cascading down the short distance to the sand. Elena fell back onto solid ground, horrified at the spectacle before her. The agonizing sounds of the avatars below filled her with panic.

The logs caught most of them as they stood in the surf. Others were pinned down on the sand.

"I didn't mean it!" Elena screamed. "I'm sorry! Can't you hear?" She hopped back and forth near the edge of the rise, overwhelmed with shock and guilt. "Get up! Please get up!" She was consumed with distress at the sounds reaching her ears from the beach. "You're getting submerged! Did you hear me? Please get up." She was choked with anguish. How could she have caused this? She wanted her companions to get up and tell her it was all right. But it was beyond her power to bring it about.

The rising tide threatened to cover those in the orange surf.

Elena worked her way down the hill, begging them to save themselves. The sounds they made carried a new tone, a desperate quality she'd never heard before.

"Matthew! Grace! Can you hear me?"

"I—I can't move, Director. My avatar, it's.... My God, we're going to drown!"

"Look around you, Grace. Can you see anyone moving?"

"The team on the beach are nearly buried, Director. And the rest of us here in the water—"

"Antonio. Can you see Antonio? Maybe he's—" The voice was cut off by a wave gently rolling over.

Elena could wait no longer. The tides were covering one of the avatars, and soon the others would be in the same situation. Disregarding the consequences, she ordered time to pause.

Wading into the surf, she worked a log off one victim, then she pulled the avatar up to the sand. Through blinding tears, Elena worked slowly and carefully. She knew there was no hurry—at least, not as far as her companions' safety was concerned. No matter what their condition was at this moment, it would remain the same until she resumed time. She made her way deeper into the orange liquid, where a raised hand signaled the location of a submerged body. The hand was clutching a large white banner that was tangled among the logs. Elena worked the avatar free and pulled it ashore.

It was the one who had been carrying the deletion tool.

Scarcely noticing her own damaged leg, she rescued one victim after another until there were no more in the surf. Up on the beach, she started removing the logs that pinned down the avatars caught there. She removed a log from one, who then remained in a sitting position, face frozen in a mask of shock. Another, with the weight removed, rolled over into a new position. Elena whimpered in misery as she surveyed the chaotic scene.

At last she could do no more; she felt consciousness slipping away from her.

She instinctively knew that if she lost consciousness during time-pause, events would resume... without her. For Elena, this would mean disconnection. If she had to lose consciousness, she knew she must first resume time.

Step by step she climbed the little hill, pausing every now and then to consider if this were the moment to resume time before it was too late. With her energy fast draining, she reached the top of the promontory, and she turned to look down once more on the group below.

Then she realized how much her avatar had suffered: when she ordered time to resume, nothing happened.

Her heart sank. She wasn't afraid of disconnection, and she knew that if she disconnected the oceans would flow again and her companions would move about. But she wanted to see them safe.

She tried to clear her mind for supreme effort. There was no urging time to start. She knew she couldn't initiate it by degrees, first slowly then fully. Time either progressed or it didn't. She had to commit completely.

Then, without knowing exactly when it happened, her mind took command....

Her companions came to life. The first one she saw stir lay face-down and pounded fists on the beach. A flood of relief settled over Elena as sounds came from the avatar.

"What's the matter with me? Somebody tell me! Am I glitching? Isaac! Robert! What's happening?"

"I'm coming, Matthew! Heaven help us—I saw it, too. We're either corrupted or those damn logs are sentient!"

"It's not the logs. How about us? How'd we get out of the water? Isaac, we're both corrupted."

"I'm telling you, it's the logs, or rocks or whatever they are. I was looking right at them. First they're on top of me, then they're piled up over there!"

"Damnit, the logs didn't pull us out of the ocean, did they? Director Patel!"

"Are you all right?"

"Yes sir, but—"

"Who saw exactly what happened?"

"I'm afraid we're not processing right, Director. Those logs—"

"I know, I know. Now compose yourselves. We've got to gather the others and exit this simulation while we still can."

"But what happened, Director?"

"Hell, Matthew, don't you think I'd like to know? Those logs are petrified code. The whole team couldn't lift one. It would take extraordinary processing power to move one of those things."

"I haven't seen anything extraordinary. Those tripods down there are so busy with their seaweed algorithms—"

"All right, let's help the others. Some of them can't walk. Where's Antonio?"

"He's sitting down there in the water, Director, laughing hysterically. Or crying. I can't tell which."

"We'll have to get him. Isaac, Robert, come along. Antonio! You all right?"

"Ha-ha-ha! Seventeen! Seventeen! Seventeen simulations, Patel, and they'll do anything I say! This one's got a mind of its own. Did you see that trick with the rocks? Ha-ha!"

"See if you can find his deletion tool, Robert; he'll either corrupt himself or one of us. Restrict his permissions and take him back to the exit portal. We'll be along shortly."

"Hee-hee! Seventeen! Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this. Ha-ha!"

Elena opened her eyes as consciousness returned. Had her companions gone?

She pulled herself along to a position between two rocks, where she could see without being seen. By the light of the twin moons she saw that they were leaving, marching away in groups of two and three, the weak helping the weaker. As they disappeared around the curving shoreline, the voices of the last two, bringing up the rear far behind the others, fell faintly on her ears over the sound of the surf.

"Is it possible that we're all corrupted, Director?"

"It's possible, but we're not."

"I wish I could be sure."

"See Antonio up ahead there? What do you think of him?"

"I still can't believe it."

"He'll never be the same."

"Tell me something. What was the most unusual thing you noticed back there?"

"You must be joking, sir. Why, the way those logs were off of us suddenly—"

"Yes, of course. But I mean besides that."

"Well, I guess I was kind of preoccupied. You know, frightened and confused."

"But didn't you notice our little glitchy friend?"

"Oh, that. I'm afraid not, Director. I—I guess I was thinking mostly of survival."

"Hmmm. If I could only be sure I saw it. If only someone else saw it too."

"I'm afraid I don't follow you, sir."

"Well, damn it all, you know that Antonio tagged it with the deletion tool. Got it in the leg. That being the case, why would the anomalous little entity come back to help us—back to us—when we were trapped under those logs?"

"Well, I guess as long as we were trapped, it figured we couldn't harm it anymore.... I'm sorry, that was illogical. I'm still a little disoriented."

"Forget it. Look, you go ahead to the exit portal and prepare for logout. I'll join you in a few minutes. I think I'll go back and look around. You know. Make sure we haven't left anyone."

"No need to do that. They're all ahead of us. I've verified."

"That's my responsibility, Grace, not yours. Now go on."

As Elena lay gathering strength for the long trek back to the hub, she saw through dimming vision one of the avatars coming back along the beach. When it was nearly directly below her, she could hear it making sounds that by now had become familiar.

"Where are you?"

Elena paid little attention to her companion's actions; she was beyond understanding. She wondered what would happen when her session expired.

"We've made a terrible mistake. We—" The sounds faded in and out on Elena's perception as the avatar turned slowly and called in different directions. She watched the avatar walk over to the pile of scattered logs and peer around and under them.

"If you're hurt I'd like to help!" The twin moons were high in the sky now, and where their light broke through the swirling clouds a double shadow was cast around the avatar. With fading awareness, Elena watched the figure shake its head slowly, then walk away in the direction of the others.

Elena's eyes stared, without seeing, at the panorama before her. The beach was deserted now, and her gaze was fixed on a shimmering white square floating on the ocean. Across it, the last thing Elena ever saw, was emblazoned the word ANTONIO.
